apoio.missao: RELIABILITAS exists to give engineering, reliability and maintenance professionals — from intern to engineer — free access, in PT and EN, to the technical knowledge usually locked behind paid standards and expensive training.
apoio.promessaDoacoes: Donations are what keep the infrastructure running.
apoio.escanearOuCopiar: Scan the QR Code or copy the code below
apoio.destinoExpansao: The idea is that collection growth is driven mainly by the users themselves: new equipment, failure modes, and more.

termos.titulo: Terms of Use and Privacy Policy
termos.usoAcesso: RELIABILITAS is an open community project on industrial reliability and maintenance knowledge, sustained by the community and by donations. Access is always free, for anyone.
termos.usoLicenca: All editorial content (the technical notes in content/) is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0). You may copy, redistribute, and adapt any note, including for commercial purposes, as long as you credit RELIABILITAS and the original author with a link to the source note, and distribute any adaptation under this SAME open license — that ShareAlike clause is what guarantees the knowledge the community builds stays open for the community. Full text: creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/.
termos.usoLicencaCodigo: The application's source code is open under the MIT license, in the same public repository as the content, on GitHub. Anyone may read, reuse, modify, and redistribute the code, with the sole requirement of keeping the copyright notice.
termos.usoConteudoItem1: Read, copy, and redistribute any note in the archive, including commercially — CC BY-SA 4.0 allows it.
termos.usoConteudoItem2: Adapt, translate, remix, or build on top of the content, as long as you distribute the result under the same CC BY-SA 4.0 license.
termos.usoConteudoItem3: Credit RELIABILITAS and the note's original author, with a link to the source page, in any reuse.
termos.usoConteudoItem4: Do not present the content as your own original work, and do not remove the original attribution.
termos.usoResponsabilidade: The content is technical reference material, synthesized from standards and established literature (see "Sources" on each page) — it does not replace the judgment of a qualified engineer applied to your specific equipment and operating context. Maintenance decisions with safety, environmental, or production impact should always go through your own professional assessment. RELIABILITAS does not guarantee the content is error-free and is not liable for decisions made based on it.
termos.usoFormularios: Both submission surfaces on the site ("Suggest a correction" and "Contribute") are moderated: every submission is reviewed by a curator before any publication. No visitor-submitted content is published automatically — and once published, it falls under the same CC BY-SA 4.0 license as the rest of the archive.
termos.privacidadeResumo: Short version: RELIABILITAS uses no tracking cookies, builds no behavioral profile, and collects no personal data by default. There is a single, functional cookie that remembers the language you picked, and an aggregate audience measurement that uses no cookie and identifies no one. The only personal information that exists is what you choose to provide, optionally, in the suggestion and contribution forms.
termos.privacidadeNaoColetaItem1: No tracking cookies, no behavioral profiling, and no selling or sharing of data with advertisers.
termos.privacidadeNaoColetaItem2: No reading preferences persisted across sessions — interface preferences (e.g., collapsed navigation tree, reading level) use sessionStorage, cleared when the tab closes.
termos.privacidadeColetaSugerir: "Suggest a correction" form: email (optional, only if you want a reply — never published) and, if you'd like credit, name, academic background, role/company, and LinkedIn/website — all optional.
termos.privacidadeColetaAutor: "Contribute" form: the same optional identification fields (name, background, role/company, LinkedIn/website), plus the contribution's own content. On both forms, two checkboxes control how this information is used: one to indicate you want to be registered as a contributor, and a separate one to authorize this information to appear publicly on the note, if it's approved and published. Legal basis: consent (you provide it actively, knowing the purpose). Retention: kept while the suggestion/contribution is under review, or until you request removal via the contact below.
termos.privacidadeColetaAutorPublico: Important — part of this may become PUBLIC: if you check the "show this information" box and the correction or contribution is approved and published, the data you fill in (name, background, role/company, LinkedIn/website) may appear as a public byline on the note. Without checking that box, the information stays with the curator only — it's never published automatically.
termos.privacidadeColetaIp: IP address (technical, transient): automatically processed by infrastructure to (a) limit abusive attempts on the 2 forms and the admin login (rate limiting), and (b) log technical errors (Sentry), when configured. It is not tied to any profile nor stored in a user table — the attempt limiter keeps this in memory, without database persistence.
termos.privacidadeTerceirosTexto: The site runs on third-party infrastructure that processes technical operational data (never personal content beyond what is described above): Vercel (hosting), Supabase (database), Sentry (technical error logging), and Cloudflare (edge protection and the aggregate audience measurement described above). The code and content are also publicly hosted on GitHub (open repository). Each provider operates under its own privacy policy.
termos.privacidadeDireitosTexto: You may request, at any time, the deletion of any personal information you provided in a form — including removing your identification from an already-published note — or ask what we have associated with you, via the contact below.
termos.privacidadeContato: Contact for privacy questions, or anything else: LinkedIn or email below.
termos.privacidadeCookieTexto: The site stores one cookie named NEXT_LOCALE, holding either "pt" or "en". It serves a single purpose: remembering the language you chose, so you are not sent back to Portuguese every time you return. It does not identify you, is not read by third parties, and does not follow your browsing on other sites. It is a functional cookie in the strict sense: without it, the language switch simply does not persist.
termos.privacidadeAnalyticsTexto: To know whether the site is being used — and nothing beyond that — RELIABILITAS uses Cloudflare Web Analytics. It measures visit counts and most-read pages in aggregate, with NO cookie, no fingerprinting, and no visitor profile: there is no way to tie a visit to a person, nor to follow anyone across sessions. It is the deliberate alternative to Google Analytics and the like, precisely so the project does not have to track anyone in exchange for knowing whether it has readers.

metodo.sub: Two frameworks in sequence: first the DIAGNOSIS of how the failure behaves over time, then the PRESCRIPTION of the task. That is how every failure mode in the collection is treated — and how the selector below decides.
metodo.aResumo: How the failure behaves over time: Nowlan & Heap pattern and Weibull β.
metodo.bResumo: The applicable and effective task: CBM, TBM, Proof Test, RTF — or redesign.

fwA.sub: How the failure behaves over time
fwA.p1: Before deciding what to do about a failure, you need to know how it happens over time. Framework A answers exactly that: does the failure mode age (wear-out), is it random, or is it most likely right after an intervention (infant mortality)?
fwA.nhP1: The classic Nowlan & Heap study (United Airlines, 1978) measured conditional probability of failure against age for thousands of items and found six patterns — with the result that redefined maintenance: only ~11% of items (patterns A, B and C) show a clear wear-out zone that justifies age-based intervention. The other ~89% are dominated by randomness or infant mortality — where scheduled overhaul does not help and can make things worse.
fwA.betaP1: The shape parameter β of the Weibull distribution turns the pattern into a number: β < 1 = infant mortality; β ≈ 1 = random (constant rate); β > 1 = wear-out. Every failure-mode note in the collection carries this reading in the purple Framework A panel — with the editorial category and the typical β cited in the literature.
fwA.betaCalc: Explore it in the Weibull calculator →
fwA.saidaP1: The output of Framework A is the input of Framework B: only after knowing whether the failure gives a measurable warning (P-F interval), whether it ages and whether operations can see it does choosing the task make sense.
fwA.irSeletor: Apply it in the strategy selector →
fwA.exemplo: Real example in the collection: Cavitation →

fwB.p1: With the diagnosis in hand, Framework B decides what to do — in the RCM order of preference (SAE JA1011; Moubray, RCM II). A task only enters the plan if it is technically APPLICABLE (detects or prevents that failure mode) and WORTH DOING (costs less than the consequence it avoids).
fwB.hierCbm: On-condition — if the failure gives a measurable warning (P-F interval), monitor the condition and act on the signal. Inspection ≤ P-F/2.
fwB.hierTbm: Scheduled restoration/discard — only when a defined wear-out zone exists (β > 1 with predictable age). Interval before the wear zone.
fwB.hierProof: Failure-finding — for HIDDEN functions (protections, redundancies): tests the function at the interval (FFI) dictated by the required availability.
fwB.hierRtf: Run to failure — legitimate when nothing above applies and the consequence is economic only.
fwB.hierRedesenho: Redesign — compulsory when the consequence is safety/environmental and no task reduces the risk to a tolerable level.
fwB.consP1: The same technical failure changes strategy with its consequence: safety/environmental demands proven risk reduction (or redesign); operational weighs downtime cost; non-operational weighs repair cost only. That is why the selector asks about consequence before closing the decision.
fwB.acervoP1: Every failure-mode note publishes with its Framework B decision and an exportable maintenance plan (green panel) — coherence enforced at build time: CBM requires a P-F interval, proof testing requires a hidden failure, RTF requires no P-F.
fwB.irSeletor: Apply it in the strategy selector →
fwB.exemplo: Real example in the collection: the Cavitation plan →

seletor.intro: Which maintenance strategy is best for my asset, given the failure mode I do not want to happen? Answer the 4 questions — the RCM decision diagram returns the strategy and the base plan. Everything runs in your browser: no data leaves this page.
seletor.q1: 1 · How does the failure behave over time? (Framework A)
seletor.q1_infantil: Infant mortality — most likely right after installation or intervention (β < 1)
seletor.q1_aleatoria: Random — constant rate, does not age (β ≈ 1)
seletor.q1_desgaste: Wear-out — ages, with predictable failure age (β > 1)
seletor.q2: 2 · Is the failure evident to operations?
seletor.q2Hint: Under normal conditions, does anyone notice the failure occurred (alarm, visible loss of function)? Protections and redundancies are usually hidden.
seletor.q3: 3 · Is there a measurable warning before failure (P-F interval)?
seletor.q3Hint: Vibration, temperature, thickness, noise, process trend — something that leaves time to act between the signal (P) and functional failure (F).
seletor.q3_nao: No — or the window is unworkable
seletor.q4: 4 · What is the worst plausible consequence?

periodicidades.pf_metade: ≤ half the P-F interval (Moubray, RCM II, ch. 8)
periodicidades.fracao_vida: before the wear zone — e.g. ≤ B10 life (Weibull)

avisos.seguranca_reduzir_risco: Safety consequence: the task must demonstrably reduce the risk to a tolerable level — otherwise combine tasks or redesign.
avisos.proof_test_seguranca_redesenho: Protection with a safety consequence: if the test interval cannot deliver the required availability, redesign is compulsory (SAE JA1011).
avisos.redesenho_compulsorio: With no applicable proactive task and a safety consequence, RCM does not accept living with the risk: a design change is mandatory.
avisos.rtf_operacional_reavaliar: RTF with relevant downtime cost: reconsider redesign or redundancy if the cost of stopping exceeds the cost of prevention.
avisos.infantil_causa_raiz: β < 1: scheduled intervention INTRODUCES failures (Nowlan & Heap). Attack the root cause — commissioning, assembly, quality — instead of overhauling by age.

guia.sub: The theory behind the three tools, what each parameter actually is, where the data comes from and how to read the results. Not everyone carries this by heart — that is what this guide is for.
guia.fluxoIntro: Each calculator answers one question of the method:
guia.fluxo1Pergunta: How does the failure behave over time?
guia.fluxo2Pergunta: How much does the failure cost in downtime?
guia.onde1: CMMS history (SAP-PM, Maximo): failure dates, operating hours and repair times.
guia.onde2: Collection notes: every failure mode cites the typical β and P-F from the literature.
guia.onde3: Industry databases (e.g. OREDA for oil & gas) when there is no own history.
guia.ondeAviso: Mistake #1: mixing different failure modes in the same sample. Each analysis uses the data of ONE failure mode.
guia.expandirDica: Click each tool to open its explanation.

weibull.pergunta: How does the failure behave over time?
weibull.teoria: Weibull describes WHEN an item tends to fail over its life — not the cost, not the detection, only the temporal pattern. Two parameters are enough: β gives the SHAPE of the failure (whether it clusters early, is random, or grows with age) and η gives the SCALE (where in time it happens).
weibull.formula: R(t) = exp(−(t/η)^β) — the chance of reaching age t alive
weibull.pBetaDesc: the SHAPE of the failure over time — this is what sets the strategy (ruler below). Dimensionless: it is the slope of the line on Weibull paper.
weibull.pEtaDesc: the SCALE: the age by which 63.2% of the population has failed, whatever the β. Carries the time unit (h, cycles).
weibull.pTDesc: the horizon you want to assess — e.g. the hours until the next scheduled shutdown.
weibull.betaIntro: β is the SLOPE of the failure rate over time — the derivative of risk. A single number says which of the three regimes the item is in, and each regime calls for a different strategy:
weibull.beta1Taxa: the failure rate FALLS with time
weibull.beta1Desc: Failures cluster early in life: manufacturing defect, assembly/installation error, bad start-up. Replacing by age does not help — it may even reintroduce the defect. The action is the root cause: quality, commissioning, assembly.
weibull.beta2Desc: The failure does not depend on age — a new item is as likely to fail as a used one. Scheduled overhaul does not reduce the rate (the dominant Nowlan & Heap pattern). Monitor the condition, if there is a P-F, or run to failure.
weibull.beta3Taxa: the failure rate RISES with age
weibull.beta3Desc: A mechanism accumulates damage: fatigue, erosion, abrasion, corrosion. There is an identifiable useful life — it makes sense to restore or discard BEFORE the wear zone (e.g. at the B10 life).
weibull.est1t: Isolate one failure mode and fix the clock
weibull.est1d: Pick ONE failure mode and the right life variable: operating hours, cycles or starts — never calendar hours. All times in the same unit and on the same clock (hour meter/PIMS, not the date).
weibull.est2t: Build the sample with failures AND suspensions
weibull.est2d: Each unit enters with a time and a label: 'failure' for those that failed by that mode; 'suspension' (right censoring) for those still running, replaced for another reason, or removed from the study. Ignoring suspensions underestimates life and distorts β and η.
weibull.est3d: Order the failure times and estimate F(t) by median rank — Bernard: (i − 0.3)/(n + 0.4) — adjusting the positions when there are suspensions (Johnson's rank). That is what linearizes the data on Weibull paper.
weibull.est4t: Fit the parameters: regression or MLE
weibull.est4d: Plot ln(t) against ln(ln(1/(1−F))): the slope is β and η is the t where F = 63.2%. With few failures or heavy censoring, prefer maximum likelihood (MLE). Software (Weibull++, R `survival`, Python `reliability`) does both and gives confidence intervals.
weibull.est5d: With fewer than ~8–10 failures the β has large uncertainty — report the confidence interval and do not decide on a knife's edge. A 'knee' in the line usually flags two mixed failure modes: go back to step 1. Without own data, start from the typical β in the collection's note and calibrate η with your plant's average life.
weibull.uso1d: β from your fit (or the typical one cited in the failure-mode note); η in hours. The colored chip beside it classifies the regime instantly.
weibull.uso2d: The decision horizon — for example, the interval until the next shutdown. It is the t inside R(t), F(t) and h(t).
weibull.uso3d: R(t) = probability of completing the mission without failing; MTTF = mean life to failure; B10 = age by which 10% have failed — the classic criterion for sizing bearings and replacements.
weibull.uso4d: If you replace or inspect every X hours, confront X with the B10 and with R(X). A low R(X), or an X beyond the B10, tell you the interval is optimistic.
weibull.uso5d: Increase η (better installation/design) or push β toward 1 (cause control) and see the effect on R(t) and B10 before committing to a plan. The resulting Fw A category feeds the strategy selector.

disp.pergunta: How much does the failure cost in downtime?
disp.teoria: For repairable items life is a cycle: operate → fail → repair → operate. Availability measures the fraction of that cycle in which the asset is fit for duty. Inherent availability (Ai) considers only the technical repair; the operational one in the field, which includes logistics and waiting, is always lower.
disp.pMtbfDesc: OPERATING hours ÷ number of failures in the period. Measures RELIABILITY (how often it fails). Never calendar hours.
disp.pMttrDesc: ACTIVE repair time ÷ number of repairs. Measures MAINTAINABILITY (how fast it returns). Technical time only — not waiting.
disp.est1t: Fix the window and the item
disp.est1d: Set the period (12–24 months give a stable sample) and the item or function under analysis. Sum the OPERATING hours over the period from the hour meter/PIMS — an asset that ran 60% of the time 'aged' 60%.
disp.est2d: MTBF = operating hours ÷ number of failures (loss of function) in the period. Exclude preventive work, process trips and interventions with no failure. And do not miss the 'small' failures operations fix without a work order — they vanish from the CMMS and inflate the MTBF.
disp.est3d: MTTR = Σ repair times ÷ number of repairs, from start of intervention to fit return. Do not include waiting for spares, travel, clearance or shift change — that is logistic time (part of MDT), a different metric. Mixing the two hides where the bottleneck is.
disp.est4t: Separate by failure mode when possible
disp.est4d: Modes with different dynamics (slow wear × sudden failure) in one MTBF become a blind KPI. One MTBF per failure mode points to action; the aggregate is only good for a report.
disp.uso1d: In the same time unit (hours). The λ = 1/MTBF appears alongside — the failure frequency.
disp.uso2d: It is the fraction of time fit for duty considering only the technical repair — the design CEILING. The availability you measure in the field will be lower, because it includes logistics and waiting.
disp.uso3d: The annual unavailability (in hours and days/year) is the number that justifies investment to management: how much production this failure+repair pair costs per year.
disp.uso4d: Compare two scenarios: doubling the MTBF (more reliability) versus halving the MTTR (more maintainability). See which moves Ai more — one of them is almost always far cheaper to achieve.

pf.teoria: A failure is rarely instantaneous: first it gives a detectable signal (point P), then it loses function (point F). This P-F interval is the window in which an inspection can catch it in time. The on-condition task is only effective if the inspection fits inside it — with slack.
pf.formula: inspection ≤ P-F / 2 — at least 2 detection chances (Moubray, ch. 8)
pf.pPfDesc: from the 1st detectable symptom (P) to loss of function (F). NOT a property of the equipment: it depends on the failure-mode + technique pair. Ultrasound/acoustic emission > vibration > temperature > noise/visual.
pf.pInspDesc: the periodicity your route practices today (weekly, monthly…). In the same unit as the P-F.
pf.est1d: The P-F changes with the instrument, not just the failure. For a bearing, ultrasound/acoustic emission sees the defect weeks before vibration, which sees it before temperature, which sees it before audible noise. Decide which technique the route will use before estimating the number.
pf.est2t: Measure the P-F in run-to-failure or history
pf.est2d: Ideally a controlled trial; in practice, use the real events that 'escaped' the route: record the time between the FIRST detectable signal (P) and loss of function (F). Collect several — the P-F has spread.
pf.est3d: Size by the pessimistic tail of the distribution, not the mean: if half the cases warn at 4 weeks and the other half at 2, design the route for 2. Conservative is correct here.
pf.est4t: No data? Use the technique's literature
pf.est4d: The collection's failure-mode notes carry the typical P-F per technique; adjust to your context (service severity, load, temperature) before settling the interval.
pf.uso1t: Enter the P-F and the practiced interval
pf.uso1d: The P-F in the chosen technique and the route's current periodicity — in the SAME unit in both fields (days, weeks or months).
pf.uso2d: It is the effectiveness ceiling: inspecting every half of the P-F guarantees at least 2 chances to catch the symptom before F.
pf.uso3t: Read the detection chances and the margin
pf.uso3d: The chances tell how many route passes fall inside the window; the margin is the slack between the window and the practiced interval.
pf.uso4t: Act if the margin is negative
pf.uso4d: Negative margin = the route cannot reach the window in time. Three ways out: increase the inspection frequency, switch to a technique with a larger P-F, or reconsider the strategy in Framework B (the on-condition task may not be applicable).

guia.fontes: Guide references: Smith — Reliability, Maintainability and Risk (2004) · Moubray — RCM II (1997), ch. 8 · Nowlan & Heap (1978). The full theory of the two frameworks lives in The method.

calc.intro: Three everyday tools for the reliability engineer — 100% in your browser: no data leaves this page.

curvaHq.titulo: Live H–Q curve — the pump in the system
curvaHq.sub: The pump does not choose where it operates: move the speed (pump curve, affinity laws) or the static head (system curve) and watch the operating point follow the intersection. Values in % of nominal BEP.
curvaHq.rotacaoSig: Affinity: Q∝N, H∝N², power∝N³ — and NPSHr also falls with N².
curvaHq.estaticaSig: Tank level, destination pressure — the part of the system curve that does not depend on flow.
curvaHq.vazaoSig: {pct}% of the current speed's BEP flow (healthy POR: 70–120%)
curvaHq.head: Head at the point
curvaHq.shutoffMsg: The pump cannot overcome the static head at this speed — zero flow (shutoff). All excess power becomes heat: the dead-heading scenario.
curvaHq.legendaModelo: Illustrative (normalized) model — does not reproduce a specific manufacturer's catalog curve.

curvaQp.titulo: Q×P — why positive-displacement pumps need a relief valve
curvaQp.sub: Close the discharge valve and compare: the rotodynamic loses flow smoothly, limited by its own curve. The positive-displacement one keeps the SAME flow — it is the pressure that spikes.
curvaQp.aberturaSig: 0% = fully closed. Both pumps face the same move — each principle's response is the opposite of the other's.
curvaQp.pressaoSig: In % of nominal pressure — without a relief valve, the weakest component in the system gives way first.
curvaQp.alertaAlivio: Above the typical relief-valve set range (~300% of nominal pressure) — real rupture risk.
curvaQp.shutoffRotodinamica: The rotodynamic pump has already stopped delivering flow (shutoff) — head levels off, it does not keep rising.
curvaQp.legendaModelo: Illustrative (normalized) model — does not reproduce a specific manufacturer's catalog curve.

weibull.invalido: Invalid inputs: β and η must be positive.
weibull.rodape: R(t) = exp(−(t/η)^β) · h(t) = (β/η)·(t/η)^(β−1). Validated against Smith (2004) and known properties (R(η)=e⁻¹). The note's editorial category prevails over this didactic reading.

sig.r: chance of passing {t} h without failing
sig.h: risk of failing in the next hour
sig.b10: age at which 10% of the population has failed

disp.rodape: Ai = MTBF/(MTBF+MTTR) — inherent availability (Smith 2004, ch. 2). Reference year: 8760 h.

sig.ai: share of time fit for duty (technical repair only)

pf.rodape: An on-condition task is only effective if inspection fits the P-F window — consecrated practice: inspection ≤ P-F/2 (Moubray, RCM II ch. 8).

sig.margem: route slack — negative = cannot get there in time

busca.dica: Try broader terms — e.g. cavitation, NPSH, bearing.

nota.anatDica: Click the numbered points to see what each component does — and where it fails.

sobre.missaoP1: Every equipment failure has a technical explanation — the problem is that explanation is rarely in one place, and most of it doesn't exist in Portuguese.
sobre.missaoP2: That's why RELIABILITAS exists: a free, bilingual digital handbook of reliability engineering and industrial maintenance.
sobre.missaoItem1: A handbook per asset: operating principle, key parts, main failure modes, and the most relevant brands/models on the market — with datasheets linked straight to the manufacturer's site.
sobre.missaoItem2: Every failure mode tied to a diagnosis and a recommended maintenance strategy, following a two-step method of its own.
sobre.missaoItem3: Three depth levels — from someone just studying the topic to someone who wants the physics and math behind the failure.
sobre.missaoItem4: A maintenance-strategy selector, reliability calculators, and more.
sobre.comunidade: It's an open community project: content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 and the code under MIT — anyone can read, reuse, and contribute.
sobre.visaoDestaque: The mid-term vision is for RELIABILITAS to become a collective reference in reliability engineering — built WITH the community. You can already contribute today: submit your own article, or suggest a correction on any note in the collection, with credit guaranteed.
sobre.linkedinSub: Send suggestions, feedback, or propose a contribution.
sobre.quemFazBio: Guilherme Joaquim Correia — mechanical engineer (CREA-SP, Brazil), with hands-on experience in industrial maintenance and planning.
sobre.quemFazHistoriaP1: The project started as personal research: gathering engineering and reliability sources, mapping isolated failure modes, trying to understand their behavior, and studying methodologies like RCM, FMEA, and RCFA — a whole world of content. An ongoing ABRAMAN certification was part of what sparked that deep dive.
sobre.quemFazHistoriaP2: From there came the idea of organizing all of it into structured material that anyone could use — not just me.
sobre.quemFazProcesso: Sources are gathered and curated with AI support, but every piece of content is reviewed, edited, and expanded before it's published.
sobre.quemFazContribuirTexto: Every note accepts suggestions for technical, visual, or structural correction — and you can also propose new content.
sobre.quemFazFechamento: Write, learn, teach — every contribution is credited to whoever wrote it.
sobre.funcionaP1: The collection is organized as a taxonomy: every equipment class and family has a seed note describing the group and the equipment that belongs to it.
